52|BACKGROUND
53|Apalutamide is an inhibitor of the ligand-binding domain of the androgen receptor.
54|Whether the addition of apalutamide to androgen-deprivation therapy (ADT) would
55|prolong radiographic progression-free survival and overall survival as compared with
56|placebo plus ADT among patients with metastatic, castration-sensitive prostate cancer
57|has not been determined.
58|METHODS
59|In this double-blind, phase 3 trial, we randomly assigned patients with metastatic,
60|castration-sensitive prostate cancer to receive apalutamide (240 mg per day) or placebo,
61|added to ADT. Previous treatment for localized disease and previous docetaxel therapy
62|were allowed. The primary end points were radiographic progression-free survival and
63|overall survival.
64|RESULTS
65|A total of 525 patients were assigned to receive apalutamide plus ADT and 527 to receive
66|placebo plus ADT. The median age was 68 years. A total of 16.4% of the patients had
67|undergone prostatectomy or received radiotherapy for localized disease, and 10.7%
68|had received previous docetaxel therapy; 62.7% had high-volume disease, and 37.3% had
69|low-volume disease. At the first interim analysis, with a median of 22.7 months of follow-
70|up, the percentage of patients with radiographic progression-free survival at 24 months
71|was 68.2% in the apalutamide group and 47.5% in the placebo group (hazard ratio for
72|radiographic progression or death, 0.48; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.39 to 0.60;
73|P<0.001). Overall survival at 24 months was also greater with apalutamide than with
74|placebo (82.4% in the apalutamide group vs. 73.5% in the placebo group; hazard ratio
75|for death, 0.67; 95% CI, 0.51 to 0.89; P = 0.005). The frequency of grade 3 or 4 adverse
76|events was 42.2% in the apalutamide group and 40.8% in the placebo group; rash was
77|more common in the apalutamide group.
78|CONCLUSIONS
79|In this trial involving patients with metastatic, castration-sensitive prostate cancer,
80|overall survival and radiographic progression-free survival were significantly longer
81|with the addition of apalutamide to ADT than with placebo plus ADT, and the side-
82|effect profile did not differ substantially between the two groups. (Funded by Janssen
83|Research and Development; TITAN ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT02489318.)

63|first prespecified interim analysis and after 83

4|Overall Survival
5|The first interim analysis for overall survival oc-
6|curred after 200 deaths were observed (83 in the
7|apalutamide group and 117 in the placebo group).
8|The overall survival percentage at 24 months
9|was 82.4% in the apalutamide group and 73.5%
10|in the placebo group (hazard ratio for death,
11|0.67; 95% CI, 0.51 to 0.89; P = 0.005), and there
12|was a 33% lower risk of death in the apaluta
13|mide group (Fig. 2A). The treatment effect on
14|overall survival consistently favored apalutamide
15|over placebo, with no significant difference in
16|the effect of apalutamide according to disease
17|volume (Fig. 2B).
18|Secondary End Points
19|The time to cytotoxic chemotherapy was signif
20|icantly longer with apalutamide than with pla-
21|cebo (Table 2, and Fig. S2 in the Supplemen-
22|tary Appendix). On the basis of the prespecified
23|hierarchical testing sequence, the time to pain
24|progression was tested next; because the between-
25|group difference did not reach statistical signifi-
26|cance, no formal testing for further secondary
27|end points was conducted.
28|Other Clinically Relevant End Points
29|The median time to PSA progression was more
30|favorable with apalutamide than with placebo
31|(Table 2, and Fig. S3 in the Supplementary Ap-
32|pendix), and PSA reached undetectable levels
33|(<0.2 ng per ml) in 68.4% of the patients in the
34|apalutamide group and 28.7% of those in the pla-
35|cebo group. A total of 87 patients in the apalu-
36|tamide group and 190 in the placebo group re-
37|ceived subsequent treatment for prostate cancer
38|(first subsequent therapies are shown in Table
39|S3 in the Supplementary Appendix). The median
40|second progression-free survival was longer with
41|apalutamide than with placebo (Table 2, and Fig.
42|S4 in the Supplementary Appendix). There were
43|few events of symptomatic local progression and
44|no substantial difference between the two groups
45|in the time to symptomatic local progression
46|(Table 2). Analysis of change from baseline in
47|the FACT-P score with the use of a mixed-effect
48|repeated-measures model showed that health-
49|related quality of life was maintained with apalu-
50|tamide, with no substantial between-group dif-
51|ference (Fig. S5 in the Supplementary Appendix).
52|Safety
53|Table 3 presents a summary of adverse events,
54|and Table 4 shows the most common adverse
55|events of any cause that occurred from the time
56|of the first dose of the trial intervention through
57|30 days after the last dose. Frequencies of grade
58|3 or 4 events (42.2% in the apalutamide group
59|and 40.8% in the placebo group) and of serious
60|adverse events (19.8% in the apalutamide group
61|and 20.3% in the placebo group) did not differ
62|substantially between the two groups. Most dis-
63|continuations of the trial intervention were the
64|result of progressive disease (in 99 patients
65|[18.9%] in the apalutamide group and 227
66|[43.1%] in the placebo group) (Table S3 in the
67|Supplementary Appendix). Adverse events led to
68|discontinuation in 42 patients (8.0%) in the
69|apalutamide group and 28 (5.3%) in the placebo
70|group (Table S4 in the Supplementary Appendix).
71|A total of 10 patients (1.9%) in the apalutamide
72|group and 16 (3.0%) in the placebo group died
73|as the result of an adverse event (Table S5 in the
74|Supplementary Appendix).
75|Rash of any grade was more common among
76|patients who received apalutamide than among
77|those who received placebo (27.1% vs. 8.5%)
78|(Table 4), and the most common adverse event
79|of grade 3 or higher that was considered by the

82|reported by 6.5% of the patients in the apalu-
83|tamide group and 1.1% of those in the placebo
84|group (Table 4); all events were grade 1 or 2.

Statistical Analysis
The TITAN trial was designed to enroll approxi-
mately 1000 patients. Radiographic progression-
free survival was tested first. If the difference
between the apalutamide group and the placebo
group was considered to be statistically signifi-
cant, the alpha was recycled to overall survival
on the basis of the fallback method.19 An overall
type I error of 5% was planned. A total of 368
events of radiographic progression were required
to provide at least 85% power to detect a hazard
ratio of 0.67 with a two-tailed significance level
of 0.005. For the final overall survival analysis,
410 deaths were required to provide approxi-
mately 80% power to detect a hazard ratio of
0.75 with a two-tailed significance level of 0.045.
Analyses of overall survival incorporated group-
sequential design with an alpha-spending func-
tion that was calculated as Wang-Tsiatis power
boundaries of shape parameter 0.2. Two interim
analyses were planned for overall survival. It was
estimated that the first interim analysis would
include approximately 50% of the total required
events for overall survival at the time of the pri-
mary analysis for radiographic progression-free
survival. The alpha level for interim analysis for
overall survival was 0.009, under the assumption
of an overall two-tailed significance level of 0.045.
Subgroup analyses were prespecified to assess
consistency of treatment effect. If the between-
group differences in the primary end points
were significant, evaluation of secondary end
points was to be performed in the following
hierarchical order, each with an overall two-
sided significance level of 0.05: time to cyto-
toxic chemotherapy, time to pain progression,
time to chronic opioid use, and time to skeletal-
related event. Demographic and clinical charac-
teristics at baseline were summarized with the use
of descriptive statistics. The primary statistical
method of comparison for time-to-event end
points was a stratified log-rank test, with strat
ification according to prespecified factors. The
Kaplan-Meier product-limit method and Cox pro-
portional-hazards model were used to estimate
time-to-event variables and determine hazard
ratios and associated confidence intervals.
Results
Patients
Between December 15, 2015, and July 25, 2017,
a total of 525 patients were randomly assigned
to the apalutamide group and 527 to the placebo
group (Fig. S1 in the Supplementary Appendix).
At the cutoff date (November 23, 2018) for the
first prespecified interim analysis and after 83
deaths in the apalutamide group and 117 in the
placebo group, the median follow-up time was
22.7 months. The median number of cycles re-
ceived was 23 for apalutamide and 19 for placebo
(range, 1 to 37 in each group). The median dura-
tion of the trial intervention was 20.5 months
for apalutamide and 18.3 months for placebo. A
total of 66.2% of the patients in the apalutamide
group and 46.1% of those in the placebo group
were receiving the trial intervention at the clini-
cal cutoff date. A total of 45 patients across the
two groups withdrew consent for the trial inter-
vention (Fig. S1 in the Supplementary Appendix).
These patients were followed for survival and
secondary end points, so their data were not
missing. A total of 39 patients were either lost to
follow-up or withdrew from all further data col-
lection; this information is not shown in Figure
S1 in the Supplementary Appendix.
Demographic and clinical characteristics at
baseline were well balanced (Table 1, and Table
S1 in the Supplementary Appendix). The median
age of the patients across both groups was 68
years. A total of 16.4% of the patients had under-

localized disease, and 10.7% had received previ-

disease, and 37.3% had low-volume disease. Pa-

disease after an initial diagnosis of localized dis-
ease; most had newly diagnosed metastatic
disease. Previous therapies for prostate cancer are

Statistical Analysis
The TITAN trial was designed to enroll approxi-
mately 1000 patients. Radiographic progression-
free survival was tested first. If the difference
between the apalutamide group and the placebo
group was considered to be statistically signifi-
cant, the alpha was recycled to overall survival
on the basis of the fallback method.19 An overall
type I error of 5% was planned. A total of 368
events of radiographic progression were required
to provide at least 85% power to detect a hazard
ratio of 0.67 with a two-tailed significance level
of 0.005. For the final overall survival analysis,
410 deaths were required to provide approxi-
mately 80% power to detect a hazard ratio of
0.75 with a two-tailed significance level of 0.045.
Analyses of overall survival incorporated group-
sequential design with an alpha-spending func-
tion that was calculated as Wang-Tsiatis power
boundaries of shape parameter 0.2. Two interim
analyses were planned for overall survival. It was
estimated that the first interim analysis would
include approximately 50% of the total required
events for overall survival at the time of the pri-
mary analysis for radiographic progression-free
survival. The alpha level for interim analysis for
overall survival was 0.009, under the assumption
of an overall two-tailed significance level of 0.045.
Subgroup analyses were prespecified to assess
consistency of treatment effect. If the between-
group differences in the primary end points
were significant, evaluation of secondary end
points was to be performed in the following
hierarchical order, each with an overall two-
sided significance level of 0.05: time to cyto-
toxic chemotherapy, time to pain progression,
time to chronic opioid use, and time to skeletal-
related event. Demographic and clinical charac-
teristics at baseline were summarized with the use
of descriptive statistics. The primary statistical
method of comparison for time-to-event end
points was a stratified log-rank test, with strat
ification according to prespecified factors. The
Kaplan-Meier product-limit method and Cox pro-
portional-hazards model were used to estimate
time-to-event variables and determine hazard
ratios and associated confidence intervals.
Results
Patients
Between December 15, 2015, and July 25, 2017,
a total of 525 patients were randomly assigned
to the apalutamide group and 527 to the placebo
group (Fig. S1 in the Supplementary Appendix).
At the cutoff date (November 23, 2018) for the
first prespecified interim analysis and after 83
deaths in the apalutamide group and 117 in the
placebo group, the median follow-up time was
22.7 months. The median number of cycles re-
ceived was 23 for apalutamide and 19 for placebo
(range, 1 to 37 in each group). The median dura-
tion of the trial intervention was 20.5 months
for apalutamide and 18.3 months for placebo. A
total of 66.2% of the patients in the apalutamide
group and 46.1% of those in the placebo group
were receiving the trial intervention at the clini-
cal cutoff date. A total of 45 patients across the
two groups withdrew consent for the trial inter-
vention (Fig. S1 in the Supplementary Appendix).
These patients were followed for survival and
secondary end points, so their data were not
missing. A total of 39 patients were either lost to
follow-up or withdrew from all further data col-
lection; this information is not shown in Figure
S1 in the Supplementary Appendix.
Demographic and clinical characteristics at

S1 in the Supplementary Appendix). The median
age of the patients across both groups was 68
